reference.source: Cummings Otolaryngology / Emery's Principles of Medical Genetics
clinicalPearls: Characterised by branchial anomalies, otological abnormalities with hearing loss, and renal malformations
Branchial defects include lateral cervical fistulae, sinuses or cysts along the line of the second branchial cleft
Otological features include preauricular pits, malformed pinnae, and hearing loss that may be sensorineural, conductive or mixed
Most commonly caused by mutations in EYA1, with SIX1 and SIX5 also implicated; inheritance is autosomal dominant with variable expressivity
Renal anomalies range from mild dysplasia to agenesis and can significantly affect prognosis, so renal imaging is essential
Temporal-bone imaging often shows cochlear hypoplasia or other inner-ear malformations
Preauricular pits with hearing loss should prompt evaluation for the full syndrome including the kidneys
reference.pathophysiology: Branchio-oto-renal syndrome results from mutations in transcription-factor and cofactor genes, most often EYA1 and the SIX family, which regulate development of structures derived from the branchial apparatus, the otic placode and the metanephric kidney. Disruption of this shared developmental network during embryogenesis produces the coexisting branchial (cleft-derived), otological (external, middle and inner ear) and renal abnormalities. Because expression is variable, affected individuals within a family can show markedly different combinations and severities of features, and penetrance is incomplete.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated branchial cleft cyst, sinus or fistula
Isolated preauricular pit or sinus without syndromic features
Other syndromic hearing loss such as Pendred or Waardenburg syndrome
CHARGE syndrome with ear and other anomalies
Townes-Brocks syndrome with ear, anal and limb anomalies
Isolated congenital renal dysplasia or agenesis
additionalInvestigations: Audiometry to characterise the type and severity of hearing loss
Renal ultrasound and further imaging to detect dysplasia, agenesis or collecting-system anomalies
High-resolution CT or MRI of the temporal bones for inner-ear malformation
Clinical assessment for branchial fistulae, sinuses and preauricular pits
Molecular genetic testing of EYA1 and related genes with family screening
redFlags: Signs of renal impairment or a solitary or absent kidney requiring nephrology input
Recurrent infection or discharge from a branchial fistula or sinus
Progressive hearing loss threatening speech development in a child
Family history of hearing loss with renal or branchial anomalies indicating dominant inheritance
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is largely determined by the severity of renal involvement, which can range from clinically silent to end-stage renal failure; hearing loss is managed with amplification or surgery, and branchial anomalies are treated surgically when symptomatic.
pitfalls: Treating a preauricular pit or branchial fistula in isolation without evaluating hearing and kidneys
Assuming normal renal function without imaging, given the wide range of renal involvement
Underestimating variability within a family and missing mildly affected relatives
Overlooking inner-ear malformations that influence surgical and rehabilitation planning
references: Cummings Otolaryngology: Head and Neck Surgery
Emery's Elements of Medical Genetics and Genomics
management: Hearing rehabilitation with amplification or cochlear implantation, and surgery to address any conductive component
Surgical excision of symptomatic branchial fistulae, sinuses and cysts
Renal surveillance and management extending to renal replacement therapy or transplantation for progressive renal failure
Temporal-bone imaging and monitoring of inner-ear malformations such as cochlear hypoplasia
Speech, language and educational support for children with hearing loss
Multidisciplinary otology, nephrology and clinical genetics follow-up
Molecular testing of EYA1 and related genes with family screening and genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance
